Done. The checkpoint event is now exactly what you described: **an event that fires off to the brain plugin, which uploads whatever the fact table holds to brainstore.** Nothing else.

What changed in the working tree (on top of the finding fix, all still uncommitted for your review):

- `memory checkpoint-work` now does **throttle → sync only**. The export and distill seams are deleted; the function and command shrank accordingly. All notify/checkpoint tests updated and green, `go vet` clean.
- The **per-chunk distill cache stays** — its honest justification today is resumed sessions: a session that ends, resumes, and ends again re-distilled its whole transcript each time, and the cache cuts that to the new tail. It's also the prerequisite for where distill is headed.
- **Where distill is headed**: your question exposed that the recorded decision 3 was wrong-shaped. With session-end deprecated and the event path distill-free, fact creation needs a home — the right one is the **memory worker** (async, leased, budgeted, already nudged by this very hint), as a durable job kind. That's now written into the design doc and COR-2127 as part of the session-end-deprecation work, not this PR.
- Updated: design doc triggers section (with the correction noted and why), table-of-truth row 3, COR-2127 title + description, Brain fact.

Why I'd built it the other way, for the record: decision 3 as we recorded it yesterday said "checkpoint is the primary trigger for *both distill and sync*." Your version is better for the reason the trail finding also found — the event path must stay cheap and agent-free, and distill timing never affects placement since facts anchor to their checkpoint whenever they're distilled.

Working tree now holds both the finding fix and this change, uncommitted. Want me to commit and push to PR #377 (I'll rewrite its body to match the reduced scope)?

input.command:
gh pr edit 377 --title "Checkpoint hint: detached fact-store upload + per-chunk distill cache (COR-2127)" --body "## Why

Facts currently reach brainstore only at session end or on a daemon tick, and developers leave sessions running for days — so a trail under review shows no memories from the work being reviewed. The host CLI now sends a detached checkpoint hint per commit (entireio/cli#2784); this PR makes the plugin upload the fact store on that beat. Part of COR-2127; design on COR-2110 (v3). Session-end is being deprecated as a trigger and nothing here depends on it.

The checkpoint event is an upload beat only: it pushes whatever facts the local store already holds. It deliberately does NOT distill — the event path stays cheap and agent-free, and distill timing never affects placement because facts anchor to their checkpoint whenever they are distilled. Fact creation stays on session-end + daemon tick and moves into the memory worker as part of the session-end deprecation.

## What changed

- **\`memory notify --event checkpoint\`** spawns a detached, hidden **\`memory checkpoint-work\`** verb (same launch shape as \`memoryWorkerLaunch\`: self re-exec, goroutine reap, worker-origin child env so nothing it shells out to re-notifies) and returns immediately. notify stays a fast content-free hint — a host adapter may invoke it synchronously. (This addresses the trail-290 review finding about inline work in notify.)
- **\`checkpoint-work\`** claims a shared 60s throttle marker under the brain write lock (claim-first, so concurrent detached hints skip instead of stampeding), then runs the existing never-fails \`hostedFactsSyncAndPull\` for the hinted branch + the default branch.
- **Per-chunk distill cache** (\`distill_cmd.go\`): the cache records each session's salted chunk content hashes; chunking is prefix-stable, so a grown transcript re-dispatches only its new tail chunks. Immediate value: a resumed session ends more than once, and each session-end re-distilled the whole transcript. Also the prerequisite for worker-driven per-checkpoint distill later. \`--force\` bypasses reuse (it drops the facts it is about to regenerate); privacy purge clears chunk records; old cache files load unchanged.

## Validation

- Tests: throttle window boundaries; branch+default sync ordering and default-only dedupe; empty-branch fallback; notify dispatches the detached verb for checkpoint and not for session_start; checkpoint-work runs the throttled sync; grown transcript re-dispatches exactly one tail chunk while earlier facts survive; \`--force\` re-dispatches every chunk.
- \`go test -race ./internal/cli\` passed on the pre-review revision (610s); the review delta is covered by the targeted suites above plus \`go vet\` and \`gofmt -s\`, and CI runs the full suite.

## Risk

Per-commit uploads are new spend on the sync path, bounded by the 60s throttle and two HTTP calls per run. No agent work and no token spend is tied to commits.

# COR-2110 table of truth

Tracks the approved decisions and their tickets. content.text:
You're right about the event path — and after the last push, the checkpoint event genuinely doesn't run distill. What's left of "distill" in PR #377 is one thing: the **per-chunk cache**, which changes how distill *re-runs*, not when it runs or what it produces. Here's exactly what it does:

**What the chunk cache does.** Distill's incremental cache used to store one fingerprint per session — a hash over the whole preprocessed transcript. If the transcript changed at all, the fingerprint mismatched and distill re-sent *every* chunk of that session to the agent again. The PR adds a second record per session: the content hashes of each chunk that was successfully distilled (salted with prompt/model/taxonomy config). On a re-run, chunks whose hash is already recorded are skipped; only unseen chunks get agent calls. Because chunking is prefix-stable — greedy by line from the transcript's start — a transcript that *grew* keeps its earlier chunks byte-identical, so a re-distill costs one tail chunk instead of the whole session. Skipping is safe because non-force distill is purely additive (facts upsert by content ID; skipped chunks' facts are already in the store, exactly your point), `--force` bypasses the reuse since it deliberately drops and rebuilds, and privacy purge clears the chunk records with the session.

**Why it exists in this PR.** Honestly: it was built for distill-on-checkpoint, which you then correctly killed. I kept it because it fixes a real, current waste that has nothing to do with the event: a **resumed session ends more than once**. Claude Code resume keeps the session ID; each session-end re-distills the whole grown transcript — today that's N agent calls for a transcript whose first N−1 chunks were already distilled. Same story when the daemon's gated distill revisits a changed session. And it's the prerequisite for the agreed end state, where distill becomes a memory-worker job firing per hint — that only has sane economics with chunk-level reuse.

**Your statement, confirmed:** the upload path never touches distill, never waits on it, and never needs it — `checkpoint-work` is throttle → `hostedFactsSyncAndPull`, full stop. The chunk cache is a sibling change riding in the same PR.

Which leaves a clean scope question: if you want #377 to be *purely* the upload beat, I can split the chunk cache into its own PR — it's self-contained (`distill_cmd.go` + `session_privacy.go` + its two tests) and stands on the resumed-session justification alone. Keeping them together is defensible too since they're both "COR-2127 fallout," but the PR title stops being the whole truth. Your call.

- Privacy purge clears chunk records alongside session entries.

- Config changes (prompt/model/taxonomy) invalidate chunk reuse: the salt is part of each chunk hash.

A transcript whose earlier content is rewritten (condense/compaction) changes those chunk hashes and honestly re-distills them — no stale reuse. The worst outcome of a corrupt/missing chunk record is one full re-distill, the previous behavior.

input.command:
gh pr edit 377 --title "Checkpoint hint: detached fact-store upload (COR-2127)" --body "## Why

Facts currently reach brainstore only at session end or on a daemon tick, and developers leave sessions running for days — so a trail under review shows no memories from the work being reviewed. The host CLI now sends a detached checkpoint hint per commit (entireio/cli#2784); this PR makes the plugin upload the fact store on that beat. Part of COR-2127; design on COR-2110 (v3).

The checkpoint event is an upload beat only: it pushes whatever facts the local store already holds. It deliberately does NOT distill — the event path stays cheap and agent-free, and distill timing never affects placement because facts anchor to their checkpoint whenever they are distilled. Fact creation stays on session-end + daemon tick and moves into the memory worker as part of the session-end deprecation. The per-chunk distill cache that originally rode in this PR is split out to #380.

## What changed

- **\`memory notify --event checkpoint\`** spawns a detached, hidden **\`memory checkpoint-work\`** verb (same launch shape as \`memoryWorkerLaunch\`: self re-exec, goroutine reap, worker-origin child env so nothing it shells out to re-notifies) and returns immediately. notify stays a fast content-free hint — a host adapter may invoke it synchronously. (This addresses the trail-290 review finding about inline work in notify.)
- **\`checkpoint-work\`** claims a shared 60s throttle marker under the brain write lock (claim-first, so concurrent detached hints skip instead of stampeding), then runs the existing never-fails \`hostedFactsSyncAndPull\` for the hinted branch + the default branch.

## Validation

- Tests: throttle window boundaries; branch+default sync ordering and default-only dedupe; empty-branch fallback; notify dispatches the detached verb for checkpoint and not for session_start; checkpoint-work runs the throttled sync.
- \`go vet\`, \`gofmt -s\` clean; CI runs the full suite.

## Risk

Per-commit uploads are new spend on the sync path, bounded by the 60s throttle and two HTTP calls per run. No agent work and no token spend is tied to commits.

**Where the event comes from and how it is triggered:**

1. `entire enable` installs a post-commit git hook that runs `entire hooks git post-commit` — this is the existing checkpoint-capture path in the host CLI.
2. Inside that flow the host calls `brainnotify.Notify`, which spawns a detached `entire brain memory notify --event checkpoint --session <id>` through the plugin dispatcher. Detached and never-fails by design: a missing or broken plugin cannot affect the commit or the hook's output. This host half exists on the **unmerged** entireio/cli branch `feat/brain-lifecycle-hints` (commit 73a92e8da) — land or re-cut it.
3. The plugin endpoint (`entire brain memory notify`, on main in `internal/cli/memory_cmd.go`) records a content-free hint and nudges the plugin's worker.
4. notify spawns a detached, hidden `memory checkpoint-work` verb (same launch shape as the memory worker; worker-origin child env for loop protection), which claims a shared 60s throttle marker and pushes the fact store for the hinted branch + default branch. Nothing heavy runs inline in notify — a host adapter may invoke it synchronously (this was also a trail-review finding on trail 290, now resolved).
5. Split into its own PR (#380 / trail 293): the per-chunk distill cache — a grown transcript re-dispatches only its new tail chunks. Immediate savings for resumed sessions that end repeatedly, and the prerequisite for later worker-driven per-checkpoint distill. Orthogonal to the upload beat; PR #377 contains no distill changes.

content.thinking:
I'm checking whether Copilot's claim holds up: that using io.Discard for stdout/stderr in SpawnDetached forces os/exec to create pipes drained by the parent, so once the parent exits the child hits a broken pipe and dies mid-work. That would mean switching to nil or real /dev/null file descriptors is the safer fix, and I want to verify this is technically accurate before accepting it.

I'm confirming this is a real, pre-existing bug in the shared SpawnDetached helper, which uses io.Discard for stdout/stderr instead of nil, and it affects other call sites like session_sweep and telemetry too. Since Wait() is never called, the parent's pipe-copying goroutines just leak harmlessly until exit, but the core EPIPE mechanism still applies — and in our case the hook process exits almost immediately after spawning the child.

The child writes "recorded checkpoint hint..." to stdout right after starting, which can easily race against the short-lived parent exiting first, killing the plugin mid-notification with SIGPIPE. This is a valid finding worth flagging as medium severity.

The fix is to set Stdout/Stderr to nil in SpawnDetached so the child gets os.DevNull instead of inheriting pipes tied to the parent — a change that benefits all three other call sites using this same detached-spawn helper, since they'd suffer the identical bug. Testing this properly is tricky since a real subprocess test is heavy-handed, and just checking that the exec.Cmd fields are nil doesn't fully verify the behavior.

That confirms it — io.Discard isn't an *os.File so it forces a pipe, while nil maps to os.DevNull. So yes, this is a valid issue affecting all four call sites in the shared helper, medium severity, fixable with a one-line change plus a comment. Since it's a clear, small fix and the user tends to want findings addressed right away, I'll answer the question and go ahead and apply the fix on the PR branch in this same turn.

I'll update spawn_detached.go to set cmd.Stdout and cmd.Stderr to nil with an explanatory comment, then add a small test by extracting a helper that builds the detached command and asserting those fields are nil. I'll leave resolving the Copilot review comment to them, just mentioning the fix in my reply.

content.thinking:
Since io.Discard isn't an *os.File, os/exec sets up real OS pipes with a goroutine draining them in the parent process. Releasing the process doesn't help since those pipe read-ends live in the parent — once the short-lived parent exits, the read ends close, so the child's next write to stdout/stderr will fail.

This explains the race exactly: the child prints "recorded checkpoint hint…" right after the parent exits and triggers EPIPE, which the Go runtime treats as a SIGPIPE kill. It's a pre-existing bug shared by all four SpawnDetached call sites, so the real fix is in the shared helper — passing nil instead of io.Discard so os/exec routes to os.DevNull directly and avoids any pipe/parent coupling at all.

Now I'm thinking through how to test this. A faithful end-to-end reproduction needs a parent that exits before its child writes, but SpawnDetached no-ops entirely under testing.Testing(), so I can't exercise the real path through the normal API. Building the actual binary for a true e2e test feels too heavy, so I'm considering pulling the command-construction logic into a separate, directly testable function instead.

Finishing the helper function that builds the detached command, then checking the existing test file for the execx package to add a test verifying Stdout/Stderr stay nil and the directory fallback works correctly.

I've confirmed the finding is valid and actually more severe than rated: using io.Discard creates OS pipes and parent-side goroutines that aren't released by Process.Release(), causing a real race where the short-lived git hook exits before the child's stdout write completes, triggering SIGPIPE and silently killing the notification — and the same bug exists in other shared-helper call sites. I'll fix it by using nil for Stdout/Stderr (avoiding pipes entirely) and write a regression test asserting those fields stay nil, since the suggested subprocess e2e test won't work due to the helper's no-op guard under `go test`.

content.text:
**Yes — valid, and I'd argue it's underrated at medium.** Fixed and pushed to #2784 (`506e8bccf`).

Why it's real: `io.Discard` isn't an `*os.File`, so os/exec silently creates an OS **pipe** per stream with the read end held by the parent — `Process.Release()` doesn't sever it. Our parent is a git hook that exits immediately, and the notify child prints "recorded checkpoint hint…" to stdout right after starting. Parent gone → pipe closed → child's write takes EPIPE → the Go runtime kills a Go process on SIGPIPE to fd 1/2. So the detached notification could die silently on the *common* path, not an edge case. Bonus: the bug was pre-existing in the shared helper — session sweep, trail-enablement refresh, and analytics spawns all carried it.

The fix: `Stdout`/`Stderr` stay `nil`, which makes os/exec open the null device *in the child* — no pipes, no parent coupling. Construction moved to a `newDetachedCmd` function so the no-parent-pipes property is unit-tested.

One correction to Copilot's suggestion, noted in the commit: its proposed "subprocess regression where the child completes after the parent exits" can't be written through `SpawnDetached` — the helper deliberately no-ops under `go test`. The testable invariant is that the constructed command holds no parent-coupled writers, which is what the new test asserts.

Worth a thumbs-up on that Copilot comment — it caught a genuine latent bug beyond the PR's own diff.

content.text:
Adversarial review done. **One high finding — confirmed and fixed** (pushed as `4daf1e544`); the rest were smaller or deliberate.

**[high, FIXED] The LookPath gate made the feature inert for the default install mode.** `main.go` prepends the managed plugin-bin dir to PATH *only* for plugin dispatch, then calls `restorePATH()` before executing built-in commands — explicitly so built-ins and their subprocesses don't inherit it. The post-commit hook is a built-in, so `exec.LookPath("entire-brain")` ran against the user's original PATH and could never find a managed install: the checkpoint hint silently never spawned for the standard flow. I verified `restorePATH()` at `main.go:87` before touching anything. Fix: the gate is gone — only the spawned `entire` child (whose own startup re-prepends) can resolve managed plugins, so a presence probe can't live in the host process at all; plugin-less machines pay one short-lived fork, the status quo. Worth owning plainly: **I introduced this bug two hours ago from the simplify review's efficiency suggestion**, whose PATH claim I half-verified — I confirmed the prepend exists but not its lifecycle. The gotcha is now a Brain fact so it doesn't bite again.

**[high→moot, FIXED] Tests stubbed the gate**, so the suite couldn't see the regression — gone with the gate.

**[medium, FIXED] Trim mismatch**: validation trimmed `sessionID`/`repoRoot` but spawned the untrimmed originals, admitting exactly the whitespace-wrapped values the guard rejected. Now trims once and uses the trimmed values; new test covers it.

**[medium, DEFERRED deliberately] Hint coverage**: hints fire only from `ManualCommitStrategy.PostCommit`'s loop — checkpoints condensed by `endSessionNow`'s eager session-end condense or recovery paths never hint and lean on the daemon tick. The right depth is the condensation chokepoint; that move is noted on COR-2127 to fold into the session-end deprecation alongside distill-into-the-worker.

**[low, moot] Per-session LookPath cost** — died with the gate.

All suites green after the fix (`brainnotify`, `execx`, strategy checkpoint tests, full `go build`). PR #2784 now stands at: ported package → simplicity pass → SIGPIPE pipe fix → gate removal. The net of all this review churn is pleasingly small: a ~55-line package with no probes, no enums, no guards beyond worker-origin and empty-input, spawning one detached argv.

I'm looking at a Trail Review finding on trail 1581, flagging that CondenseSession gets called from sibling paths in ManualCommitStrategy that also produce durable canonical checkpoints but never emit hints, which echoes but sharpens the earlier adversarial review's concern about hints only coming from PostCommit.

The sharper claim here is that once a session gets marked FullyCondensed, PostCommit's loop skips it entirely on a later pass, meaning that session's checkpoint can never retroactively get a hint — leaving an entire class of sessions (file-less or ended early) permanently hint-less. I'm checking the actual skip condition at the top of the loop to verify this claim is accurate.

But thinking through impact: today this gap doesn't actually matter in practice, because sessions ending without a subsequent commit still get their facts synced via the session-end hook's own hosted sync path. The gap only becomes real once session-end is deprecated, which is precisely when the design calls for the hint to move to the condensation chokepoint or memory worker — so this is better treated as an intentional, documented scope decision rather than an accidental gap.

I'll add a brief comment at the call site explaining this deliberate scope — commit-beat coverage only, with session-end and daemon reconciliation covering the rest until the hint relocates — then resolve the trail finding with that explanation, since the finding itself treats documentation as an acceptable resolution.

content.thinking:
I've confirmed the skip location, both lifecycle call sites, the sweep, and the snapshot path, so the finding holds up factually. Now I'm weighing whether this is actually a design flaw: the hint exists for the commit beat, signaling that a commit landed and the fact store should be uploaded alongside it, whereas the sibling paths it references create checkpoints without any commit involved—like the session-end eager condense, which is already handled by its own export hook.

The background sweep, late subagent capture, and manual checkpoint snapshots don't involve a commit either, so there's nothing for facts to trail alongside; the daemon tick already keeps uploads fresh. This means the gap is intentional for now and only becomes real work once session-end is deprecated, which the ticket already tracks. Since the finding itself accepts documenting the scope decision as a valid resolution, I'll add a scope comment at the call site, push the change, and resolve the finding.

Confirmed: the skip logic is correct, but the fact that condensation/checkpoint paths never trigger a hint is intentional yet undocumented — which is exactly what the reviewer flagged. I'll make that scope decision explicit in code (with the real fix tracked under COR-2127) and then resolve the finding.

content.thinking:
The user wants to know whether the daemon is per-repo or global, and whether it could watch git refs directly instead of being triggered by the CLI. I recall the daemon runs via launchd with a label like io.entire.brain-watch.a2d3fd66 based on earlier status output.

So it seems like there's one watch daemon per repo, identified by a repo-specific hash in the label. Looking at the watch mechanism, it polls on an interval (default 5 minutes) and fingerprints checkpoint refs plus HEAD rather than using filesystem events, which means the daemon already watches the refs itself and triggers factsSync with a 15-minute throttle. The CLI-triggered event mainly exists to close the latency gap between the 5-minute poll and near-instant notification, and to cover cases where the daemon isn't installed or running.

I'm weighing whether FS-based watching (inotify/FSEvents) could replace the polling approach, but packed-refs makes ref watching unreliable since loose refs can get packed by git gc, and cross-platform file watching adds real dependency complexity that the existing polling solution avoids. Also, the CLI event carries the session ID directly, whereas a ref watcher would need to reverse-engineer which session triggered a change from checkpoint metadata — plus daemons can simply not be running, as is the case on this very repo, making the CLI-triggered hint path more reliable since it works with zero daemon dependency.

So the daemon is per-repo (a launchd agent keyed by repo-path hash), opt-in, and often not installed — it already handles reconciliation via throttled tick-fingerprint polling of checkpoint refs and HEAD. Making it the primary channel instead of a fallback would mean either accepting slow polling latency or taking on fragile cross-platform FS watching, and losing the free session ID the host already provides. The event path is the zero-infrastructure option — exact timing, exact session, no daemon required — while the daemon tick serves as the reconciliation floor underneath it. I want to verify the per-repo claim by checking how the watch daemon is labeled and installed in the entire-brain code.

This daemon is actually opt-in and currently not installed on this machine, meaning it's often absent. Watching repo refs already effectively happens through polling — fingerprinting checkpoint refs and HEAD per tick triggers a refresh with a 15-minute throttle — but switching to real event-latency FS-watching would require the daemon to always exist and would be unreliable given loose files, packed-refs rewrites, and inconsistent OS watch APIs, whereas the CLI hint works with zero resident infrastructure.

So the two channels don't compete — the event gives precise, fast, zero-infra notification carrying the session ID, while the daemon tick acts as a reconciliation floor catching missed events and daemon-only setups. That's the current design; killing the CLI event would mean making the daemon mandatory, which is a product call since setup is opt-in today.

content.text:
**One global daemon per machine, not per repo.** `setup` installs a single supervised service (launchd label `io.entire.brain-watch.<hash>` — the hash is of the daemon *name* for label uniqueness, not a repo). It runs `entire-brain workspace watch` with no argument, which watches **every repo recorded in the machine-level watch plan**, each with its own interval, distill cadence, and budget. One process, N repos.

**It already watches the repo refs — by polling.** Each tick fingerprints the checkpoint refs + HEAD per repo; a changed fingerprint triggers the refresh, and the hosted facts sync runs on a 15-minute throttle. So "daemon watches refs" isn't hypothetical, it's the existing reconciliation floor.

Could it *replace* the CLI event? Three reasons I'd say no:

1. **The daemon is opt-in and often absent.** It only exists after someone runs `setup` with the daemon install — on this very machine, `brain status` reports `daemon.installed: false`. The CLI hint works with zero resident infrastructure: the notify child launches the worker on demand and exits. Making the daemon the only channel makes freshness depend on an install step most repos haven't done.
2. **Event-latency ref watching is genuinely messy.** To get seconds instead of poll-minutes, the daemon would need OS file watching on `.git` ref paths — and git refs are hostile to watchers: checkpoint refs live as loose files until git packs them into `packed-refs`, so a watcher must handle loose-file events, whole-file packed-refs rewrites, and three OS watch APIs, across every repo in the plan. The polling fingerprint exists precisely to avoid that.
3. **The event carries information the refs don't.** At PostCommit the host knows *which session* condensed into the checkpoint and hands it over in the argv. A ref watcher sees "something moved" and must re-derive session membership from checkpoint metadata — fine for a plain upload, but it throws away the precision we'll want when distill moves to the worker and runs per checkpoint.

So the architecture we landed on is the two channels composing: **event = fast path** (seconds, exact session, no daemon required), **daemon tick = floor** (catches missed events, covers commit-less facts, works for people who never commit from a hooked repo). If you ever want to delete the event channel, the prerequisite is a product decision to make the daemon mandatory — at which point poll latency vs. FS-watch complexity becomes the real trade, not the spawn.

content.text:
Default tick is **every 5 minutes** (`--interval`, `watch.go`). But the tick is cheap — the real work runs on throttles layered on top of it:

| Work | Default cadence |
|---|---|
| Poll tick (fingerprint checkpoint refs + HEAD) | 5 min |
| Deterministic refresh | on fingerprint change (free, no tokens) |
| Full consolidation (heavy refresh) | ≥ 30 min (`--consolidate-every`) |
| Hosted facts sync | ≥ 15 min (`hostedSyncMinInterval`) |
| Distill / seed agent steps (token-spending) | off by default; when enabled, ≥ 24 h (`--distill-every`), budget-capped |

In supervised mode each workspace in the machine watch plan can carry its own values for these. So worst-case freshness via the daemon alone is ~5 minutes to notice a change plus the 15-minute sync throttle — which is exactly the gap the per-commit hint (seconds, 60s throttle) closes.

There's a design question raised: the checkpoint hint fires on the local post-commit hook, so facts get uploaded to brainstore before that commit is even pushed to remote, meaning the trail wouldn't yet have that commit. I'm thinking through whether that's actually intended, since facts uploaded at local commit time reference commit C via anchors, and the trail page needs to join against those anchors.

Though trail membership only updates on push, so a pre-push fact just sits unattached in brainstore until the push happens -- but I realize there's a subtler case: if a fact is anchored to a session rather than a specific commit, and earlier checkpoints of that session were already pushed, the fact could surface on the trail via session-join even before its own commit lands. That raises a privacy question about exposing work-in-progress to teammates, though I note this isn't actually new behavior since hosted sync already uploads facts on session-end regardless of push status.

I'm also weighing whether pre-push upload is even necessary, given that teammates' pull filters use reachability so unpushed commits can't pollute their local brains anyway -- which makes me consider hinting on the push hook instead of post-commit, since the trail only updates at push time regardless, though I still need to think through what commit-time timing buys over push-time.

since commit-anchored facts can't attach until push anyway, only a session-level join could surface them pre-push, so the pre-push timing is inherited harmlessly from existing sync design. It could ride the existing pre-push hook for fewer events, trading minor loss of facts between last push and abandonment for earlier off-machine durability — an acceptable trade. As for watching repo refs directly instead of a daemon, I already covered that: opt-in global daemon polling every 5 minutes.

Now I'm thinking about whether a true event system could replace the daemon spawn entirely. A unix socket requires the daemon to be running and discoverable; a simpler option is a file-based queue where the host just appends a hint line to a well-known file and never spawns a process — the daemon drains it on its next tick, or any plugin invocation picks it up. That file-append approach seems like the cleanest middle ground: content-free, cheap, no spawn at all.

The real tradeoff is latency: without an installed daemon, pickup only happens on next use or tick, losing the near-instant feedback that motivated the original design — so a hybrid where the host spawns only if no daemon is detected might be worth the added complexity. I'm also preparing an honest response to the team, conceding that pre-push upload probably isn't needed for the trail UI and that push-beat timing would work just as well if we move the call site.

I'll give my assessment directly in chat and offer to post it to the PR thread if useful. I should also flag switching the trigger to push as a genuine option worth considering, laying out the trade-offs for the team to decide rather than prescribing an answer — keeping things plain and structured around the two questions raised.

content.text:
Good feedback — both points deserve straight answers, and one of them exposes a real design choice we should make explicitly.

**1. "Do we need to send info to the trail before commits reach the remote?"**

No — the trail UI can't use it early anyway, and that's worth conceding. A trail learns about commit C at *push*; a fact anchored to C that arrives in brainstore pre-push just sits there until the push lands and the join starts matching. So commit-beat uploads buy the trail page nothing over push-beat uploads. Two clarifications that matter, though:

- **Pre-push upload is not new in this PR.** The hosted sync has uploaded facts on session-end and the 15-minute daemon tick since COR-2030, with no relationship to push. The hint only changed *latency*, not the privacy posture. And teammates can't see unpushed work early regardless: their pull filter keeps a fact only if its anchor commit is reachable from their HEAD — unpushed commits aren't.
- **The trigger could ride the push beat instead.** The host already owns a `pre-push` hook. Moving the hint there covers the reviewer use case exactly (facts arrive when the trail can first attach them), fires less often than per-commit, and drops the "uploads work that's never pushed" noise. What commit-beat buys over it is only earlier off-machine durability of facts and a head start of a few seconds. I'd call push-beat the better fit for the stated goal — happy to move the call site; it's a one-line relocation plus test updates.

**2. "One daemon per repo or global? Could it watch repo refs instead? Ideally an event system that doesn't spawn a process."**

- **Global**: one machine-wide supervised daemon (launchd/systemd), watching every repo in the machine watch plan. It *already* watches the repo refs — by polling: 5-minute tick fingerprints checkpoint refs + HEAD, hosted sync throttled to 15 minutes. And it's **opt-in**: it only exists after `setup` installs it (it isn't installed on this machine right now). Making ref-watching the only channel means making the daemon mandatory — a product decision, not a wiring change — and either accepting poll latency or taking on FS-watching git refs across three OSes, which packed-refs makes genuinely unpleasant.
- **On "an event system always means spawning a process"**: that's almost exactly right, and the reason is structural — kubectl-style plugins have no resident endpoint, so *something* must wake the plugin up. The no-spawn design exists: the host appends a content-free line to a hint file the plugin owns, and whoever next wakes (daemon tick, any plugin invocation) drains it. That's zero coupling and zero forks — but without a resident daemon, nothing wakes up, so latency falls back to the 5-minute tick. The spawn isn't incidental coupling; it's the wake-up primitive in a daemon-optional world. If the team is comfortable with "seconds-fresh only when the daemon is installed, minutes otherwise," hint-file + daemon is the cleaner architecture and we can delete the spawn.

So the two real options to put to the team: **(a)** keep the spawn but move it to the push beat (less chatty, same decoupled shape, works daemon-free), or **(b)** hint-file consumed by the daemon/next-invocation (no spawn at all, but freshness depends on the daemon being installed). I'd take (a) now and revisit (b) when the daemon install story changes.

Want me to post this as a reply on the PR thread so the team sees the trade-offs in place?

content.text:
The anchor point exists: the git `pre-push` hook runs `entire hooks git pre-push`, which calls `strategy.PrePushFromGitHook` — the step that pushes the **checkpoint refs** alongside your branch. That's exactly the right neighbor for the hint. Here's the full timeline:

**The sequence on `git push`:**

1. You run `git push`. Git invokes the pre-push hook **before any ref leaves your machine**, handing it the list of branches being pushed.
2. The host does its existing work (ship checkpoint refs), then fires the detached hint — cost to the push: one `fork`, microseconds. Because the hook's exit code can abort the whole push, the hint stays detached and never-fails, same contract as before.
3. **Two transfers now race in parallel:** (a) the git push + platform ingest (commits, checkpoints, trail create/update), and (b) the plugin's fact upload (throttle check → `hostedFactsSyncAndPull`, two HTTP calls, typically sub-second).
4. The trail page is a read-time join, so whichever side lands last completes the picture. In practice (b) finishes before the platform has ingested the push, so **by the time the trail first shows the new commits, their memories are already in brainstore** — from the reviewer's perspective, facts and commits appear together.

**Worst cases, all bounded:**
- Upload slower than ingest → the trail shows commits a few seconds before their memories. The join self-heals; nothing is misplaced.
- The hint process dies, or the push is rejected after the hint fired → facts were uploaded for unpushed work. Same posture as today's session-end/tick uploads: invisible to teammates (reachability filter), attaches whenever the push eventually lands; the 15-min daemon tick remains the floor for a lost hint.
- Burst of pushes (rebase + force-push loops) → the 60s throttle marker collapses them.

**What this deliberately doesn't change:** fact *creation* timing. Distill still runs at session end / daemon tick until it moves into the worker — so a push mid-session uploads previously distilled + `remember`ed facts; the in-flight session's facts follow at its end. Also strictly fewer events than commit-beat: one hint per push instead of per condensed session per commit.

**One contract change rides along:** at pre-push there's no "the session that condensed" — the hint carries just the branch. Today the plugin's `memory notify` requires `--session`. Cleanest: add a `push` event to the plugin's accepted set (`--event push --branch B`, no session, skips the per-session hint record, goes straight to the throttled upload), and the host sends that instead of `checkpoint`. Honest naming, no fake session IDs.

Change set: host — move the call from `PostCommit`'s loop to the pre-push hook command (one hint per pushed branch), `NotifyCheckpoint` → `NotifyPush(repoRoot, branch)`, tests follow; plugin (#377) — accept `--event push` without `--session`, dispatch `checkpoint-work` on it, tests follow; the PostCommit scope comment and PR bodies update to match. Say go and I'll make the move on both branches.

content.thinking:
The teammate's idea is to have entire-brain install its own git pre-push hook chained alongside the host's, reusing the cli's existing hook-chaining logic, rather than embedding brainnotify code directly in the cli. This keeps plugin-specific logic separate until a proper messaging system exists. Since the user is asking for my assessment here, I should focus on evaluating the approach rather than jumping into implementation.

Weighing it honestly: this would let entire-brain's setup fully own the pre-push hook, dispatching its own upload command without the cli needing any brainnotify package, plugin-name knowledge, or env-var contract. That would eliminate the coupling objection entirely, kill PR #2784's whole review tail, and remove version-skew concerns between cli and plugin since the plugin wouldn't need a cli release to ship.

The tricky part is hook chaining — git only runs one pre-push file, and the cli currently owns and idempotently reinstalls that file via `entire enable`, so I need to understand whether the cli already supports chaining to other hooks (a teammate mentioned it does) or whether entire-brain would risk clobbering the existing hook on reinstall.

Also need to consider stdin handling, since pre-push hooks receive ref lines on stdin and a proper chain would need to tee that to each sub-hook, though entire-brain's branch resolution logic probably doesn't need it. Beyond that, adding a git hook per repo means entire-brain's setup now owns new surface area: install, idempotence, uninstall on disable, and doctor checks.

For the actual invocation, timing and semantics stay identical — still a detached spawn on pre-push. But I'm hitting the same PATH gotcha as before: the plugin binary likely isn't on PATH for managed installs, so the hook needs either a baked absolute path recorded at install time, or to dispatch through the "entire brain" wrapper that resolves managed installs. Baking the path is simpler but risks breaking across plugin upgrades.

My verdict sides with the teammate — this is the better near-term shape, since it converts a cross-repo cli-plugin contract into a plugin-internal feature. The process-coupling concern the teammate raised still technically exists since the hook always spawns a process, but now both ends belong to the plugin, which is really the point. Before committing I should verify what the cli's actual chaining mechanism is, so the new hook integrates properly rather than wrapping blindly — and I need to think through consequences for the in-flight cli PR, which would mostly need to close unmerged.

The one piece worth salvaging from the cli PR is the SIGPIPE fix, a genuine pre-existing bug affecting the cli's own call sites — that deserves its own small PR separate from the rest, which can close. The entire-brain PR keeps its existing value (notify, push-work, throttled upload) while gaining the hook installer, either folded in or as a follow-up commit. Right now neither repo has clean committed state: the cli worktree has the NotifyPush move staged but uncommitted, and the plugin workspace has the push-event rename and push-work changes sitting uncommitted in the working tree, since I was interrupted before committing cli first.

Good thing the user denied that last cli commit attempt — it aligns with this new direction. Now I want to check the cli's hook-chaining mechanism concretely, looking at how the installed hook script is generated via the git hook command helper and whether it properly chains to any pre-existing hooks.

content.thinking:
I'm confirming that the CLI backs up any pre-existing foreign hook with a ".pre-entire" suffix and chains to it, so entire's hook wraps whatever was already installed. That means install order matters for entire-brain's chaining to work correctly, depending on which hook gets installed first.

If entire enable runs first, then entire-brain's installer needs to detect entire's existing hook, back it up, and chain to it the same way. But this gets tricky on re-installs or upgrades — since the active hook (brain's wrapper) doesn't itself carry the entireHookMarker, even though the backup file it chains to does, the CLI's InstallGitHook logic might mistakenly treat brain's hook as foreign and back it up again under ".pre-entire", potentially creating a chain loop or redundant backup.

This could result in double execution: brain's wrapper chaining to the old entire backup while the new entire hook also runs, effectively running entire's hook logic twice on each push — wasteful even if idempotent. I'm thinking the simplest fix is to just copy the CLI's existing backup-and-chain approach for brain, but I need to consider whether brain should instead append its logic into the CLI-owned hook file directly — though that risks the CLI's content-comparison check silently stripping brain's addition on the next enable run.

Actually, maybe brain shouldn't chain at all in that case — if brain skips chaining when it detects entire's marker, entire's hook is only lost until the next enable, which seems like an acceptable tradeoff given that the CLI's chaining logic was really designed for wrapping foreign hooks like husky, not a sibling tool that also reconciles files. The pragmatic fix: brain only installs its own hook when none exists or wraps a genuinely foreign one, and defers entirely when it detects the entire marker already present.

A cleaner middle path occurs to me though: have the cli ship a generic, plugin-agnostic chain line in its generated hook — something that sources a local hooks directory or file if present — giving every plugin, including brain, a stable slot to drop its own script into without the cli needing any specific knowledge of brain itself.

That said, the teammate's pushback was even stronger: they suggested the cli needs zero changes at all, since it already has chaining logic brain can simply copy for its own hook setup. I should agree with killing brainnotify and letting the plugin own its hook, but flag the real risk — that cli-managed hook reconciliation plus mutual wrapping could cause double-execution or get silently reverted, so install ordering needs care — then offer the two possible implementation shapes.

Tracing through the double-execution risk: if cli's hook chains to its backup (brain's wrapper), and brain's wrapper also chains to the old entire hook, then entire's pre-push logic could run twice. The fix for option A is to have brain's wrapper avoid preserving a stale chained copy and instead delegate directly to the current guarded entire hook invocation, so it stays in sync rather than duplicating work.

But that creates a worse problem: since both cli and brain each try to reconcile the same hook file, they'd keep detecting each other's modifications as "foreign" and re-wrapping, causing an infinite reconciliation fight. I'm concluding there's no clean way to let brain own this file without touching `core.hooksPath`, which would be even worse since it relocates every hook, not just pre-push. So a plugin-owned hook with no cli cooperation inherently has this failure mode when `entire enable` re-triggers the wrap/rewrite cycle.

Given that pre-push failures can abort pushes outright under OPF's privacy semantics, a doubled or mangled chain carries real risk, not just cosmetic duplication. The real fix is option B: cli owns a generic five-line dispatcher that execs everything in a `pre-push.d` directory, so cli stays the sole owner of the hook file while brain just drops a file into that directory — no reconciliation conflict, and nothing plugin-specific lives in cli itself. This matches what the teammate actually wants: a generic hooks.d mechanism rather than plugin-specific code baked into cli, essentially a lightweight messaging system for now. I should write up the assessment and recommendation along these lines.

For in-flight work, this means closing most of #2784 while keeping the execve SIGPIPE fix as its own PR since it addresses cli's existing spawns independently, and plugin #377 stays mostly unchanged aside from how the hint sender works. I shouldn't implement anything until the team picks A or B, since this is a real team-contract decision the teammate needs to weigh in on — I just need to present the tradeoffs clearly.

content.text:
The direction is right and I'd take it — it deletes the cross-repo contract entirely. But I checked how the cli's chaining actually works, and there's one real hazard the "just copy the chaining code" framing glosses over:

**How cli chaining works:** `entire enable` owns the hook *files*. When it finds a pre-existing foreign hook, it backs it up (`.pre-entire` suffix) and writes its own hook with a `# Chain: run pre-existing hook` call to the backup. Crucially, enable also **reconciles**: a hook file whose content doesn't match what it expects gets rewritten. That's built for wrapping husky-style foreign hooks once — not for a *sibling tool that also reconciles the same file*.

**The hazard:** repos are typically entire-enabled first. So entire-brain's installer would wrap the cli's hook (back it up, chain to the backup). - Pagination: every list takes an opaque cursor and returns next_cursor when more remains — exhaust the pages before concluding "that's all".
- Time: since/until are ISO 8601 / RFC3339 bounds; where offered, timeframe is a relative window (last-month, last-3-months, last-6-months).
- Size: reads that can be large (files, diffs, transcripts) honor max_tokens and return next_cursor to continue — raise max_tokens or page rather than assuming truncation is the whole story.

- sessions[].tokenUsage on a checkpoint is a PER-CHECKPOINT delta, not a session total — sum across a session's checkpoints, or use get_entire_session for the authoritative total.

# MCP Server Instructions

The following MCP servers have provided instructions for how to use their tools and resources:

## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. ## claude.ai Datadog
This is an MCP server for Datadog (a software observability platform). See Datadog docs if you're unsure about how something works in the platform. Docs for this MCP server can be found at https://docs.datadoghq.com/bits_ai/mcp_server/setup/ MCP write tools are omitted because your organization has MCP Write Access disabled. An organization administrator can enable MCP Write Access in Organization Settings. Reconnect afterward so your client refreshes its tools. This server ships skill guides containing domain-specific guidance, workflows, and best practices that are not visible in tool names or schemas. Before invoking other tools, always perform skill discovery by running both paths in parallel: a direct load with `load_datadog_skill` using a general domain name (e.g. skill_name='datadog/traces'), and a call to `list_datadog_skills` with a fuzzy `query` based on topic keywords — load any clearly matching result from the listing along with the related skills it points to. The exception is a follow-up call in a domain whose skill you have already loaded or confirmed absent this session. If nothing clearly fits, do not load a skill — proceed with the tool descriptions. When the user asks to visualize, chart, or graph data — or when loading a data domain skill (e.g. datadog/traces, datadog/logs, datadog/metrics) — also load datadog/visualizations. Investigation results often benefit from charts.

## claude.ai entire-prod-us
Entire MCP — an investigation surface over Entire's engineering data: repos and their analytics, git history (commits, files, trees, refs, diffs), the AI checkpoints and sessions behind the code (with transcripts and token accounting), trails (PR-like change proposals), and code search. Reads are curated `*_entire` tools; a small write/ops group covers trail/review/runner/dispatch mutations.

Workflow: when you only have a repo name, path, or URL, call resolve_entire_repo first, then pass the repo it returns to repo-scoped tools. Prefer the aggregation tools (get_entire_repo_overview, get_entire_my_activity) over hand-rolling stats from raw listings.

Querying conventions (shared by every tool):
- Addressing: name a repo by a prefixed path (gh/<owner>/<repo>, et/<project>/<repo>, git/<owner>/<repo>) or a repo ULID. Repo ULIDs are REGION-SCOPED — the same repo has a different ULID per region, so never carry a ULID across regions or sessions; if a tool rejects one, re-resolve with resolve_entire_repo.
- Pagination: every list takes an opaque cursor and returns next_cursor when more remains — exhaust the pages before concluding "that's all".
- Time: since/until are ISO 8601 / RFC3339 bounds; where offered, timeframe is a relative window (last-month, last-3-months, last-6-months).
- Size: reads that can be large (files, diffs, transcripts) honor max_tokens and return next_cursor to continue — raise max_tokens or page rather than assuming truncation is the whole story.

Pitfalls:
- sessions[].tokenUsage on a checkpoint is a PER-CHECKPOINT delta, not a session total — sum across a session's checkpoints, or use get_entire_session for the authoritative total.

\`SpawnDetached\` set Stdout/Stderr to \`io.Discard\`. A non-\`*os.File\` writer makes os/exec allocate an OS pipe per stream, drained by a goroutine in the **parent**; \`Process.Release\` does not sever that. Once a short-lived parent — a git hook — exits, the pipe read ends close, the child's next stdout/stderr write takes EPIPE, and the Go runtime kills a Go child on SIGPIPE to fds 1/2: the detached work dies mid-flight. All three call sites (session sweep, trail-enablement refresh, analytics) carry this today.

## What changed

\`Stdout\`/\`Stderr\` stay \`nil\`, so os/exec opens the null device **in the child**: no pipes, no parent coupling. Command construction moves to \`newDetachedCmd\` so the no-parent-pipes property is unit-testable — a subprocess e2e through \`SpawnDetached\` is not possible because it deliberately no-ops under \`go test\`.

## Validation

\`go test ./cmd/entire/cli/execx\` passes (new tests assert nil output streams and the cwd fallback).

Part of the COR-2110 design (v3). The push is the moment the platform learns a branch's commits, so it is the upload beat: a pre-push hook tells the plugin, and the plugin uploads whatever the fact store already holds — detached, throttled, no distill anywhere in the event path. Fact creation stays on session-end + daemon tick and moves into the memory worker with the session-end deprecation.

**Ownership (decided with soph, 2026-10-15): everything lives in entire-brain; the cli is untouched.** Earlier iterations put a `brainnotify` sender in the cli (post-commit, then pre-push) — cli PR #2784 is closed; only its standalone execx detached-pipe fix survives as cli #2789.

**How it works:**

1. `entire brain setup` (and `connect`) installs the plugin's own `pre-push` hook, chained beside whatever hook owns the slot, using the cli installer's pattern (hooks.go#L780-838) adapted for a guest of the slot: wrap a foreign hook (back it up by MOVE and `exec` it with original stdin/args so its exit code still decides the push), never re-claim the primary after `entire enable` re-wraps ours, `$0`-relative chain so a relocated copy self-disables instead of double-running the host's hook. The reconcile-side fix for wrapped-hook cycles is being handled in the cli separately (soph).
2. The hook body runs the plugin by its baked absolute path (git hooks get the user's PATH; managed installs are not on it), backgrounded with all stdio detached: `entire-brain memory notify --event push`. It cannot consume the pre-push ref list, slow the push, or fail it.
3. `memory notify --event push` (no session — a push has no single session) spawns the hidden `memory push-work` verb detached, which claims a shared 60s throttle marker under the brain write lock and runs the existing never-fails `hostedFactsSyncAndPull` for the current + default branch.
4. `setup --uninstall` removes the hook and restores anything it chained to; `disconnect` wiring is a one-line follow-up once this branch rebases over COR-2109 (the hook is already a no-op for opted-out repos — the sync gates on the binding).
5. Ships alongside: the per-chunk distill cache (PR #380 / trail 293) — orthogonal; resumed sessions stop re-distilling their whole transcript.

Daemon tick stays as reconciliation for missed hints and commit-less facts.

python3 - <<'PY'
# Design doc: triggers section → plugin-owned pre-push hook.
p='.context/cor-2110-memories-trails-design.md'
s=open(p).read()
old_start=s.find('The checkpoint event (post-commit hook) is an **upload beat only**')
old_end=s.find('## Implementation tickets')
assert old_start!=-1 and old_end!=-1
new_triggers='''The push is the upload beat, and the trigger is **entire-brain's own pre-push git hook** — the cli is untouched (decided with soph 2026-10-15; two earlier iterations put a sender in the cli on post-commit, then pre-push, both superseded). The hook uploads whatever facts the local store already holds; it never distills. Fact creation stays on the session-end hook and the daemon tick, and moves into the memory worker with the session-end deprecation.

- **Install**: `brain setup` and `brain connect` install the hook, chained beside whatever hook owns the slot, using the cli installer's pattern (hooks.go#L780-838) adapted for a guest: wrap a foreign hook (back it up by move, `exec` it with original stdin/args so its exit code still decides the push), never re-claim the primary after `entire enable` re-wraps ours, and a `$0`-relative chain line so a relocated copy self-disables instead of double-running the host's hook. The cli-side reconcile fix for wrapped-hook cycles is soph's, separate.
- **Hook body**: runs the plugin by its baked absolute path (git hooks see the user's PATH; managed installs are not on it), backgrounded with all stdio detached: `entire-brain memory notify --event push`. It cannot consume the pre-push ref list, slow the push, or fail it.
- **Plugin**: `memory notify --event push` (sessionless — a push has no single session) spawns the hidden `memory push-work` verb detached; it claims a shared 60s throttle marker under the brain write lock and runs the never-fails `hostedFactsSyncAndPull` for the current + default branch.
- **Timing**: the fact upload races the git push + platform ingest; both are a few seconds, so memories appear on the trail together with the commits. A rejected push uploads facts for commits that land later — invisible to teammates (reachability filter), same posture as the session-end/tick uploads that always ran pre-push.
- **Daemon tick** stays as reconciliation for missed hints and commit-less facts; **connect** doubles as first pull. `setup --uninstall` removes the hook and restores anything it chained to.

'''
s=s[:old_start]+new_triggers+s[old_end:]
s=s.replace('5. COR-2127 — host `brainnotify` + checkpoint-event upload trigger (sync only; distill moves to the memory worker with the session-end deprecation) + the per-chunk distill cache.',
            '5. COR-2127 — plugin-owned pre-push hook → `memory notify --event push` → detached throttled upload; the per-chunk distill cache ships separately (PR #380).')
open(p,'w').write(s)

# Table of truth row 3 + current line.
p='.context/cor-2110-table-of-truth.md'
s=open(p).read()
s=s.replace('| 3 | Checkpoint event (post-commit hook → host `brainnotify` → plugin notify) is an upload beat: detached sync of the existing fact store, no distill in the event path; distill moves to the memory worker with the session-end deprecation |',
            '| 3 | The push is the upload beat: entire-brain installs its OWN chained pre-push hook (cli untouched) → `memory notify --event push` → detached throttled sync of the existing fact store; no distill in the event path; distill moves to the memory worker with the session-end deprecation |')
old_cur=s[s.find('Current: COR-2127'):s.find('\n\n| #')]
new_cur='''Current: COR-2127 — In Review (2026-10-15): entire-brain #377 (push event + push-work + plugin-owned pre-push hook installer), entire-brain #380 (per-chunk distill cache), cli #2789 (execx detached-pipe fix — the only cli change that survived; #2784 closed after the team moved hook ownership into the plugin). Trail-290 finding resolved. Crosses off on merge; distill-into-memory-worker and disconnect-hook-removal are follow-ups with the session-end deprecation / COR-2109 rebase.'''
s=s.replace(old_cur,new_cur)
open(p,'w').write(s)
print("docs ok")
PY

1	# Design: how memories attach to trails (COR-2110)
2	
3	Version 3, approved 2026-10-14. Owner: evis. Implementation tickets: COR-2123 to COR-2127. Versions 1 and 2 are summarized at the end.
4	
5	## Summary
6	
7	A fact records which session, checkpoint, and commit produced it. These provenance anchors are written at creation and never change. Every consumer — the trail page, the repo Memories page, and a teammate's local brain — selects facts by querying these anchors. The branch name is not a key anywhere. Sync is per-fact: the client upserts facts up, and pulls a repo-wide delta down, filtered locally by git reachability from its own HEAD. Upload runs on the checkpoint event (per commit), on session end, and on the daemon tick.
8	
9	## Problem
10	
11	Memories are keyed by branch name at every layer:
12	
13	- Local store: `facts/<slug>-<sha256(branch)[:4]>/facts.ndjson` (`internal/cli/facts.go`).
14	- Sync protocol: `GET/POST /api/v1/repos/{repoID}/brain/facts?branch=<name>` (`internal/factsync/httpserver.go`), one CAS set-head per `(repo, branch)`.
15	- Brainstore: `branch` is in the primary key of `brain_fact_heads`, `brain_facts`, and `brain_fact_events`. `/memories` filters `WHERE repo_id = $1 AND branch = $2`.
16	
17	Branch names change. Three failure modes, all reported:
18	
19	1. Rename (Conductor renames placeholder branches automatically): local facts stay in the old directory; the hosted head stays under the old name; the new name starts empty.
20	2. Delete after merge: the rows still exist under the old name, but no caller holds that name, so the trail UI gets an empty list.
21	3. Recycle: a new branch that reuses a deleted name syncs against the old head. The first pull imports the old facts into the new local store, and new facts publish into the old head.
22	
23	A fourth problem surfaced during this design: with per-branch heads and no promote step, facts synced under a feature branch never enter the `main` head, so a teammate on main never receives them locally after the trail merges. Version 1 papered over this with a promote-on-merge event. Version 3 fixes it structurally.
24	
25	## Facts about the current system that the design uses
26	
27	- Fact identity is `sha256(normalized text + sorted paths)`. Branch is not part of the identity (`factmerge/record.go`).
28	- Fact status moves one way: active → superseded/retracted. Never back.
29	- Distill stamps each fact with provenance anchors: SessionID, CheckpointID, transcript position (`internal/cli/distill_cmd.go:1133`). It does NOT stamp `Anchor.Commit` today; only authored facts get a commit (`rememberAnchorCommit`, `internal/cli/facts_write_cmd.go`). The design requires distill to also stamp the commit, resolved from the fact's OWN checkpoint via the `Entire-Checkpoint` commit trailer (the entity index already builds this mapping from git log) — never from HEAD: a background distill of an old session must anchor to that session's historical commit, not whatever is currently checked out. An unresolvable checkpoint leaves the commit blank; an absent anchor is honest, a wrong one is not (same rule as `rememberAnchorCommit`). Part of COR-2126.
30	- Anchors cross the wire. `SanitizeForEgress` removes only the local transcript path and line; SessionID, Commit, CheckpointID, and TurnID stay in the synced blob (`internal/factsync/egress.go`).
31	- Brainstore currently drops anchors when it projects the blob into `brain_facts` rows.
32	- The platform already maps checkpoints and sessions to trails. Trails have stable ULIDs.
33	- The client has the full commit graph. Reachability (`git merge-base --is-ancestor`) is a cheap local check. The server does not need the git graph for anything in this design.
34	
35	## Design
36	
37	One rule everywhere: a fact is selected by its anchors, never by a branch name.
38	
39	Ingestion is one funnel: `remember` and distill (kept as-is — decided 2026-10-14) both write the local fact store. The fact store pushes to brainstore on post-commit. Every view — trail page, repo page, teammate pull — selects from brainstore by anchors, so a trail shows exactly the facts whose checkpoint/commit is on it and everything else falls out.
40	
41	### Storage (brainstore)
42	
43	Per-fact rows keyed `(repo_id, fact_id)`, plus anchor rows (fact_id → SessionID, CheckpointID, Commit, TurnID). No set heads, no CAS, no `branch` column in any key. Branch may be stored as display metadata on an anchor.
44	
45	Writes are idempotent upserts: anchors union, status advances one way, text/paths are fixed by the content-derived ID. Two clients upserting the same fact converge without coordination. Conflicting facts (two active facts that disagree) are stored side by side; resolution belongs to the planned async pipeline, same as before.
46	
47	One denormalization: a `trail_id` column, stamped on a fact when its trail merges (from the trail-merge event, by matching the fact's anchors to the trail's membership), and on upsert when an arriving fact's anchors belong to an already-merged trail — a session that ends after a squash merge uploads facts anchored to the trail's checkpoints, and the merge-time stamp alone would miss them. It gives cheap trail filtering and carries the repo-page backlink below. The anchor join stays the source of truth; `trail_id` is a materialized copy of its result.
48	
49	### Sync protocol (replaces `facts?branch=` / `facts/advance`)
50	
51	- **Push:** `POST /repos/{id}/brain/facts:upsert` with a batch of facts + anchors. Idempotent. Server stamps attribution from the token, as today.
52	- **Pull:** `GET /repos/{id}/brain/facts?since=<cursor>` — a repo-wide delta feed ordered by `updated_at`. Pagination is the platform standard: opaque cursor in, `next_cursor` out (internally a keyset over `(updated_at, fact_id)`, the same shape brainstore's `/memories` already uses). Nothing new is invented. Status changes bump `updated_at`, so retractions re-deliver through the same feed. Resync = omit the cursor and replay from zero (client applies are idempotent); a cursor that predates a schema migration gets a reset error. No branch parameter.
53	- **Client-side filter on pull:** keep a fact if any anchor commit is reachable from local HEAD, or any anchor session is one of this member's sessions, or the fact has no session/commit anchors (repo pool). Everything else is cached or skipped per client policy.
54	
55	The old protocol and `factmerge`'s set-level CAS/merge path are retired. The e2e-validation condition for replacing the protocol was met on 2026-10-08, and exposure is still off behind `trail-memories`, so the replacement cost is at its minimum now.
56	
57	### Why rename, delete, recycle, and merge stop being cases at all
58	
59	- Rename/delete: no storage is keyed by the name, so there is nothing to strand or orphan.
60	- Recycle: the new branch's history does not contain the old trail's commits, so the old facts fail the pull filter. If the old trail merged, its commits are in the new branch's history and its facts pass the filter — which is correct, not contamination.
61	- Merge: with a true merge, the trail's commits become ancestors of main and the facts pass every main-based filter directly — repo page and teammate pulls. With a squash merge they do not; the `trail_id` backlink stamped at merge covers that case, and the pull filter treats a fact with a merged `trail_id` as main-visible. The stamp is a cache of the join, so a missed merge event degrades to the session-join path, never to wrong placement.
62	- Closed without merge: the commits never reach main, so the facts never pass a main-based filter. They remain visible on the closed trail.
63	- A lost event delays an upload. It cannot misplace a fact, because selection is computed from stored anchors at read time.
64	
65	### Attachment (which trail or page shows a fact)
66	
67	- A fact belongs to trail T if any anchor references a session, checkpoint, or commit in T. The UI renders the fact next to the commit its anchor points to.

git add internal/cli/memory_cmd.go internal/cli/memory_notify_sync.go internal/cli/memory_notify_sync_test.go internal/cli/memory_lifecycle_regression_test.go internal/cli/push_hook.go internal/cli/push_hook_test.go internal/cli/setup.go internal/cli/connect_cmd.go && git commit -m "push beat: plugin-owned pre-push hook uploads the fact store

The push is the moment the platform learns a branch's commits, so it is
the upload beat — and per team decision the whole trigger lives in this
plugin; the host CLI is untouched (its PR 2784 is closed, superseded by
this).

- push_hook.go installs our own pre-push hook, chained beside whatever
  hook owns the slot, adapting the host installer's pattern for a GUEST
  of the slot: a foreign hook is backed up by MOVE and exec-chained with
  the original stdin, args, and exit code; after 'entire enable'
  re-wraps our hook we never re-claim the primary (re-claiming would
  ping-pong with its reconcile); and the chain line is \$0-relative, so
  a relocated copy self-disables instead of double-running the host's
  privacy-critical pre-push. Wired into setup, connect, and
  setup --uninstall (restoring anything we chained to). Disconnect
  wiring follows the COR-2109 rebase; the hook is already a no-op for
  opted-out repos because the sync gates on the binding.

- The hook body runs this plugin by its baked absolute path (git hooks
  see the user's PATH; managed installs are not on it), backgrounded
  with all stdio detached: it cannot consume the pre-push ref list,
  slow the push, or fail it.

- memory notify accepts --event push: sessionless (a push has no single
  session, so no lifecycle record and no worker nudge), it spawns the
  hidden 'memory push-work' verb detached, which claims a shared 60s
  throttle marker under the brain write lock and runs the never-fails
  hostedFactsSyncAndPull for the current + default branch. Nothing in
  the event path distills; fact creation stays on session-end + tick
  until it moves into the memory worker.

Part of COR-2127 (COR-2110 design v3).

gh pr edit 377 --title "Push beat: plugin-owned pre-push hook uploads the fact store (COR-2127)" --body "## Why

The push is the moment the platform learns a branch's commits, so it is the upload beat: facts should arrive in brainstore as the commits arrive on the trail. Per team decision (soph), the whole trigger lives in this plugin — the host CLI is untouched (cli#2784 closed; its standalone execx fix survives as cli#2789). Part of COR-2127; design on COR-2110 (v3).

The event path never distills: it uploads whatever the fact store already holds. Fact creation stays on session-end + daemon tick and moves into the memory worker with the session-end deprecation. The per-chunk distill cache is #380.

## What changed

- **\`push_hook.go\`**: installs our own \`pre-push\` hook (wired into \`setup\`, \`connect\`; removed by \`setup --uninstall\` and \`disconnect\`, restoring anything we chained to). It adapts the host installer's pattern (cli hooks.go) for a **guest** of the slot: a foreign hook is backed up by move and exec-chained with the original stdin, args, and exit code — its verdict still decides the push; after \`entire enable\` re-wraps our hook we never re-claim the primary (re-claiming would ping-pong with its reconcile); the chain line is \`\$0\`-relative, so a relocated copy self-disables instead of double-running the host's privacy-critical pre-push. The cli-side reconcile fix for wrapped-hook cycles is handled separately (soph).
- **Hook body**: runs this plugin by its baked absolute path (git hooks see the user's PATH; managed installs are not on it), backgrounded with all stdio detached — it cannot consume the pre-push ref list, slow the push, or fail it.
- **\`memory notify --event push\`**: sessionless (a push has no single session — no lifecycle record, no worker nudge); spawns the hidden **\`memory push-work\`** verb detached, which claims a shared 60s throttle marker under the brain write lock and runs the existing never-fails \`hostedFactsSyncAndPull\` for the current + default branch. (This shape also resolves the trail-290 finding about inline work in notify.)

## Validation

- Installer tests: empty slot, idempotent rerun, chaining a pre-existing hook verbatim with exec semantics, host-re-wrap left alone, uninstall restores the original.
- Event tests: only \`push\` dispatches; throttle window boundaries; branch+default ordering and default-only dedupe; empty-branch fallback; push-work command runs the throttled sync.
- Full \`go test -race ./internal/cli\` green before the rebase onto main (COR-2109 merge); targeted suites + \`go vet\` + \`gofmt -s\` green after, including the updated connect banner test.

## Risk

A rejected push still uploads facts for commits that land later — invisible to teammates (reachability filter), identical posture to the session-end/tick uploads that always ran pre-push. Hook coexistence with \`entire enable\` re-wrapping is deliberately one-sided: we never fight for the slot; worst case our hint stops firing until the next setup/connect, and the daemon tick covers it.

gh pr create --base main --head memory-trail-attachment-design --title "Push beat: plugin-owned pre-push hook replaces the checkpoint event (COR-2127)" --body "## Why

Follow-up to #377, which merged the checkpoint-event upload beat (host-notified via the now-closed cli#2784). The team decision landed after that merge: the trigger moves to the **push** (the moment the platform learns the commits) and lives **entirely in this plugin** — the cli keeps no brain-specific code. This PR transforms the merged state into that final shape.

## What changed

- **\`push_hook.go\`** (new): installs our own \`pre-push\` hook — wired into \`setup\`, \`connect\`; removed by \`setup --uninstall\` and \`disconnect\` (restoring anything we chained to). Guest-of-the-slot chaining, adapted from the cli installer's pattern: a foreign hook is backed up by move and exec-chained with the original stdin, args, and exit code; after \`entire enable\` re-wraps our hook we never re-claim the primary; the \`\$0\`-relative chain self-disables when relocated, so we cannot double-run the host's privacy-critical pre-push. The cli-side reconcile fix for wrapped-hook cycles is handled separately (soph).
- **Hook body**: runs this plugin by its baked absolute path (git hooks see the user's PATH; managed installs are not on it), backgrounded with all stdio detached — it cannot consume the pre-push ref list, slow the push, or fail it.
- **\`memory notify\`**: \`--event push\` (sessionless) replaces the checkpoint dispatch; it spawns the hidden \`memory push-work\` verb (renamed from \`checkpoint-work\`), same claim-first 60s throttle + never-fails \`hostedFactsSyncAndPull\` for current + default branch. \`checkpoint\` returns to a pure hint record.
- Connect banner mentions the push beat; its test updated.

## Validation

- Installer tests: empty slot, idempotent rerun, verbatim chain of a pre-existing hook with exec semantics, host-re-wrap left untouched, uninstall restores the original.
- Event tests: only \`push\` dispatches; throttle boundaries; branch+default ordering/dedupe; empty-branch fallback; push-work runs the throttled sync.
- Full \`go test -race ./internal/cli\` green pre-rebase; targeted suites + \`go vet\` + \`gofmt -s\` green on the rebased head.

## Risk

A rejected push still uploads facts for commits that land later — invisible to teammates (reachability filter), same posture as session-end/tick uploads. Hook coexistence with \`entire enable\` is deliberately one-sided: we never fight for the slot; worst case the hint pauses until the next setup/connect and the daemon tick covers it.

The push is the moment the platform learns a branch's commits, so it is the upload beat: a pre-push hook tells the plugin, and the plugin uploads whatever the fact store already holds — detached, throttled, no distill anywhere in the event path. Fact creation stays on session-end + daemon tick and moves into the memory worker with the session-end deprecation.

**Ownership (decided with soph, 2026-10-15): everything lives in entire-brain; the cli is untouched.** Earlier iterations put a `brainnotify` sender in the cli (post-commit, then pre-push) — cli PR #2784 is closed; only its standalone execx detached-pipe fix survives as cli #2789.

**How it works:**

1. `entire brain setup` (and `connect`) installs the plugin's own `pre-push` hook, chained beside whatever hook owns the slot, using the cli installer's pattern (hooks.go#L780-838) adapted for a guest of the slot: wrap a foreign hook (back it up by MOVE and `exec` it with original stdin/args so its exit code still decides the push), never re-claim the primary after `entire enable` re-wraps ours, `$0`-relative chain so a relocated copy self-disables instead of double-running the host's hook. The reconcile-side fix for wrapped-hook cycles is being handled in the cli separately (soph).
2. The hook body runs the plugin by its baked absolute path (git hooks get the user's PATH; managed installs are not on it), backgrounded with all stdio detached: `entire-brain memory notify --event push`. It cannot consume the pre-push ref list, slow the push, or fail it.
3. `memory notify --event push` (no session — a push has no single session) spawns the hidden `memory push-work` verb detached, which claims a shared 60s throttle marker under the brain write lock and runs the existing never-fails `hostedFactsSyncAndPull` for the current + default branch.
4. `setup --uninstall` removes the hook and restores anything it chained to; `disconnect` wiring is a one-line follow-up once this branch rebases over <issue id="995a1543-56ff-4846-a15f-98049539cabc" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-2109/brain-connectdisconnect-easy-user-facing-commands-for-hosted">COR-2109</issue> (the hook is already a no-op for opted-out repos — the sync gates on the binding).
5. Ships alongside: the per-chunk distill cache (PR #380 / trail 293) — orthogonal; resumed sessions stop re-distilling their whole transcript.
